title: How to Use Covered Calls to Generate Monthly Income
description: A beginner's guide to 'renting out' your stocks for extra cash flow.
content:
Most investors think the only way to make money from stocks is for the price to go up (Capital Appreciation) or for the company to pay you (Dividends). There is a third way: **Selling Options**. Specifically, the 'Covered Call' strategy allows you to 'rent out' your shares to other investors in exchange for a cash premium. It is widely considered the safest options strategy, often used by retirees to boost income from a stagnant portfolio. This guide explains how to turn your 100 shares of stock into a monthly paycheck.

Key Takeaways

  • The Mechanism: You agree to sell your shares at a higher price (Strike Price) in the future. In exchange, you get paid cash today (Premium).
  • The Requirement: You must own 100 shares of the underlying stock to sell 1 contract. You cannot do this with 50 shares.
  • The Risk: Capped Upside. If the stock moons (e.g., goes up 20% in a month), you miss out on the profit above your strike price. You never lose your principal, only the 'opportunity' of a massive rally.
  • Income Generation: In a flat or slightly bullish market, covered calls can generate 1-2% monthly income on top of dividends.

Why It Matters (US Context)

In the US, options premiums are generally taxed as Short-Term Capital Gains (ordinary income rates) unless held for long periods, which is rare for covered calls. Holding the underlying stock in a tax-advantaged account (IRA) makes this strategy extremely efficient.

Anatomy of a Covered Call

Scenario: You own 100 shares of Apple (AAPL) at $150/share. Total value: $15,000.

The Trade

You sell (write) a "Call Option" with a $160 Strike Price expiring in 30 days.
The buyer pays you $200 Premium instantly.

Outcome A: Stock stays below $160

At the end of 30 days, Apple is at $155.
The option expires worthless. You keep your 100 shares. You keep the $200.
Result: You made $200 profit on a stock that didn't do much. You can now repeat this next month.

Outcome B: Stock rises to $170

The option is "In the Money". You are forced to sell your shares at $160.
You keep the $200 premium. You keep the profit from $150 to $160 ($1,000).
Missed Opportunity: You missed the gain from $160 to $170. You still made money, just less than if you had just held.

Execution Strategy

  1. Accumulate 100 Shares: This is the barrier to entry. You cannot sell calls on VTI if you only own 50 shares.
  2. Choose a Delta: Look for a 'Delta' of 0.30. This suggests a ~70% probability that the option expires worthless (you keep the stock). It strikes a balance between income and risk of assignment.
  3. Avoid Earnings: Do not sell calls during earnings week. Volatility can cause the stock to spike, causing you to lose your shares.
  4. The 'Wheel' Strategy: Advanced investors combine this with 'Cash Secured Puts' to buy stocks at a discount and sell them at a premium repeatedly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I lose money?

Only if the stock price crashes. If Apple drops to $100, you still own the shares (now worth less). The premium you collected ($200) actually cushions the blow slightly. It is safer than just holding.

What if I want to keep the stock?

Then don't sell calls. Or, if the price rises, 'Roll' the option (buy it back and sell a new one at a higher price/later date) to avoid selling shares.

Is this passive?

No. It requires monthly management. ETFs like JEPI or QYLD do this for you automatically for a fee, but DIY yields are often better.
